hook_text: That R90 bag of coal actually costs R97. The other R7? Someone downwind is quietly paying it.
clip_script: A coal depot on the edge of a township, trucks rolling from before dawn. Coal sells at ninety rand a bag — and at ninety it sells mountains. Now stand one street downwind. Dust on the washing, so families buy more soap. Windowsills repainted a year early. Children with tight chests: inhalers, clinic queues, taxi fare. Add it up honestly and every bag costs the neighbours about seven rand in coping. But no invoice for that seven rand ever arrives at the depot. The buyer across town pays ninety and thinks that's what coal costs. It isn't. A bag costs ninety-seven — ninety at the gate, seven in soap, paint and inhalers, paid by people who never bought coal at all. And here's what the lying price does: because coal looks seven rand cheaper than it truly is, people buy MORE of it. The market over-produces exactly the thing that coats the township — not from cruelty, from a bill that was never sent. Flip it: a boxing gym in a container keeps teenagers off the corners and the whole street calmer — benefits nobody pays the gym for. So at sixty rand a month, too few join. One unsent bill makes too much coal dust; one unsent thank-you makes too few boxers. That is market failure — and the fix starts with making the price tell the truth.
visual_style: A split-screen township scene in muted dawn colours: coal trucks and drifting dust on one side, a container gym glowing warm on the other; animated invoices float off the dust and the gym and dissolve before reaching anyone's hands.
mood: Grounded and quietly indignant, resolving into clear-eyed insight.
pacing: Slow build through the downwind costs, a sharp price-reveal beat at ninety-seven, then a brisk mirrored flip to the gym and a tight closing line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to see how taxes, subsidies and cost-benefit analysis make lying prices tell the truth.
